על בסיס הפרשנות הכפולה, המאמר מראה כיצד העולם המדעי מפספס את החיבור הקריטי הזה בשל הקריאה השגויה של פרק א' כרצף פיזי. פרקים ב' ו-ג' מתוארים כשיאו של התהליך: תיאור ההתגלמות הפיזית של התודעה (כתנות עור) וכינון האדם כישות מודעת באמצעות השגת ה ״דעת טוב ורע״. בניתוח זה, מוצעת פרספקטיבה תיאולוגית-פסיכולוגית חדשנית, המציבה את הכתובים כמקור לגיטימציה תיאולוגית לתהליכים האבולוציוניים, ובכך מאפשרת לאחוז יחד בנרטיב הרוחני המכונן ובמציאות המדעית-האבולוציונית של קיום האדם.

English Abstract: This article proposes a revised and systematic reading of the Creation Story in the Book of Genesis (Chapters 1–3), seeking to bridge the historical gap between the traditional religious narrative and scientific/evolutionary findings.


The central thesis posits that the Creation Story is divided into two distinct and parallel narratives:


1. Chapter 1 is not a chrono-physical description, but an allegory for the development of collective human consciousness ("Elohim")—from the moment of awakening out of the "Tohu V'Vohu" (chaos) to the fundamental ability to perceive and make basic distinctions (light/dark, land/sea).


2. Chapter 2 serves as a parallel narrative describing the physical chronology of the creation of the world and man ("YHWH Elohim"), revealing a sublime compatibility with the scientific evolutionary sequence: from a world of land and water, through the hydrological cycle and the emergence of flora, and finally to the creation of 'Adam' as a 'living soul' (early life/mammals).


Based on this dual interpretation, the article demonstrates how the scientific world misses this critical connection due to the flawed reading of Chapter 1 as a physical sequence. Chapters 2 and 3 are depicted as the culmination of the process: the description of the physical embodiment of consciousness (the 'garments of skin') and the establishment of man as a conscious entity through the attainment of 'the knowledge of good and evil'.


This analysis offers a novel theological-psychological perspective, positioning the Scriptures as a source of theological legitimation for evolutionary processes, thereby allowing the spiritual narrative and the scientific-evolutionary reality of human existence to be held in harmony.

title: Reconstructing the Law of Supply and Demand: A Unified Dynamic Framework for Micro and Macro Economics and Its Policy Applications

detail.title: Reconstructing the Law of Supply and Demand: A Unified Dynamic Framework for Micro and Macro Economics and Its Policy Applications
detail.abstract: Traditional economic theories, relying on homogeneous agents and static equilibrium assumptions, fail to adequately explain structural unemployment and income polarization under technological shocks. This paper proposes a dynamic framework based on heterogeneous agents to reconstruct the law of supply and demand. It analyzes how technological advancements affect income distribution, labor markets, and overall economic development. By introducing the willingness-to-pay ordering model, the marginal cost staircase model, and the skill threshold model, the paper explores how technological advancements influence workers across different income groups and skill levels. Using empirical data from multiple countries, the paper provides theoretical support for policies aimed at achieving inclusive growth and discusses how education, technology, and international trade policies can be coordinated to address technological shocks.

title: N m'a faamu. Boosting Learning Through Bilingual Education: Evidence from Mali

detail.title: N m'a faamu. Boosting Learning Through Bilingual Education: Evidence from Mali
detail.abstract: Despite increased school enrollment across Sub-Saharan Africa, learning outcomes remain critically low. In this paper, I explore the replacement of colonial languages as the primary medium of instruction in Africa as an educational intervention designed to enhance student learning. This study evaluates the long-term impacts of Mali's 1999 national bilingual education reform, which introduced 11 local languages into the primary school curriculum as languages of instruction. Exploiting spatial variation in policy implementation and using a difference-in-differences approach with commune-level data, the study finds that exposure to bilingual education significantly improves local language literacy by 30% and French literacy by 10%, and increases school attendance by 5 percentage points. These gains are especially pronounced among women and individuals with educated mothers. Contrary to concerns over national cohesion, the policy does not exacerbate ethnic tensions. The findings contribute to the literature on large-scale bilingual education and the political economy of language use in Africa, suggesting that integrating local languages into education systems can enhance human capital without undermining nation-building.

detail.abstract: Related party transactions (RPTs), once a key expropriation channel in Chinese business groups, have sharply declined under strict regulation. However, controlling shareholders circumvent these rules. We provide systematic evidence that these shareholders tunnel resources from listed parent firms to "dual-identity subsidiaries" (DISs), non-wholly owned subsidiaries in which these shareholders also hold minority stakes, through unregulated, undisclosed transactions. In China’s top 300 listed firms, DISs show 66% higher profitability and 64% higher dividend payouts than non-DISs do. Using Bertrand et al. (2002)’s approach, we attribute the superior performance of DISs to tunneling, revealing continued shareholder expropriation beyond regulated RPTs.

title: GDP Alternatives Revisited: a systematic review of barriers to the adoption of alternative measures of economic progress
affiliations: University of the District of Columbia and University of the District of Columbia

detail.title: GDP Alternatives Revisited: a systematic review of barriers to the adoption of alternative measures of economic progress
detail.abstract: For almost a century, the United States and countries around the world have measured their economic progress through the Gross National Product (GNP) and its close relative, the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). GDP measures the final goods and services produced in a country or region in monetary units. Neither positive nor negative social and environmental impacts of economic activity are included in the measure. There is a considerable body of work arguing that GDP is not a measure of social welfare and distorts the impact of economic activity Given its well-documented shortcomings, a plethora of alternative measures have been developed to correct the welfare distortions of GDP. Collectively they are known as Beyond GDP (BGDP) measures. However, to date, none of the alternatives proposed over the past 50 years have been widely adopted. This study examines the lack of progress toward the adoption of an alternative measure to GDP using a systematic review of the BGDP literature as its starting point for examining barriers to the adoption of BGDP measures. We found that only 2.4% of the considerable literature on BGDP measures includes discussion of adoption barriers. This lack of consideration of practical operational issues stands out. Our review finds five key issues that constitute barriers to adopting a GDP alternative: 1) the inability to shift paradigms 2) the misalignment of data needs and public sector structures 3) the lack of resources, 4) the lack of a cohesive communication strategy, and 5) the lack of user training.

title: Adoption Is Not Enough: A Behavioral Perspective on the Imperfect Substitution of Green Alternatives
affiliations: ESCP Business School and Catholic University of Louvain (UCL)

detail.title: Adoption Is Not Enough: A Behavioral Perspective on the Imperfect Substitution of Green Alternatives
detail.abstract: Companies increasingly pursue economic and environmental goals simultaneously through the development of green products, services, or business models. However, the environmental savings of such green alternatives depend on their substitution effect. This paper explores this often-overlooked contingency by drawing on theories of behavioral change to explain how substitution ratios may be improved. After reviewing several alternative theories of behavioral change, we evaluate their ability to explain carsharing’s substitution for private cars. We find that some individual intentions are associated with increased substitution while others are not, resulting in inconsistent behavior. Moreover, our results point to the importance of changes in context in shaping substitution ratios.

title: On the Heresthetics of Salience: Competing over Voters’ Attention

detail.title: On the Heresthetics of Salience: Competing over Voters’ Attention

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates a voting model in which two candidates strategically compete in a winner-take-all election. Voters consider both the spatial dimension of policy positions and other attributes, or valence, of each candidate. Candidates are policy motivated and endeavor to make specific attributes ”salient” in voters’ minds by leveraging their comparative advantages to influence the voting outcome - a form of ”heresthetic” behaviour. The paper offers three contributions. First, it characterizes Salient Political Equilibria and suggests ways in which the notion of salience can be made operational. Second, it provides novel experimental evidence supporting voting salient behaviour. Third, it offers empirical evidence that candidates internalize the externality that ensues from voters salient behaviour, in the context of the European migration crisis of 2015. The theoretical, experimental, and empirical findings challenge the conventional median voter paradigm and its implications by highlighting the significant impact of voters’ salience on electoral outcomes.

title: Generative AI and Firm Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail

detail.title: Generative AI and Firm Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We quantify the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) on firm productivity through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading cross-border online retail platform. Over six months in 2023-2024, GenAI-based enhancements were integrated into seven consumer-facing business workflows. We find that GenAI adoption significantly increases sales, with treatment effects ranging from 0% to 16.3%, depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to existing firm practices. Because inputs and prices were held constant across experimental arms, these gains map directly into total factor productivity improvements. Across the four GenAI applications with positive effects, the implied annual incremental value is approximately $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. The primary mechanism operates through higher conversion rates, consistent with GenAI reducing frictions in the marketplace and improving consumer experience. We also document substantial heterogeneity: smaller and newer sellers, as well as less experienced consumers, exhibit disproportionately larger gains. Our findings provide novel, large-scale causal evidence on the productivity effects of GenAI in online retail, highlighting both its immediate value and broader potential.

title: Shift or Share? Anatomy of Profit Shifting and Distributional Effects on Workers
affiliations: , Paris School of Economics (PSE),  and

detail.title: Shift or Share? Anatomy of Profit Shifting and Distributional Effects on Workers

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using exhaustive microdata on the worldwide activity of multinational firms from Country-by-Country Reports linked to employer-employee data, we study how profit shifting affects workers' earnings. We estimate that large French multinationals shift 19% of their foreign profits annually to low-tax jurisdictions, resulting in €10.3 billion shifted out of France and €3.7 billion in lost tax revenues. Exploiting France's mandatory profit-sharing policy, which mechanically links subsidiary-level reported profits to workers' compensation, we show that profit shifting reduces annual employees' earnings by 2.6%. Low-income workers are disproportionately affected, the bottom 10% losing 3.2% of wages compared to 2.3% for top 10% earners. Changing the profit-sharing formula to account for global, rather than subsidiary-level, profitability would increase wages by 1.9% overall and 4.1% for workers in profit-shifting subsidiaries.

title: Equilibrium Trade Regimes: Power- vs. Rules-Based
affiliations: , University of Turin and Sao Paulo School of Economics

detail.title: Equilibrium Trade Regimes: Power- vs. Rules-Based

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Members of the World Trade Organization are increasingly disregarding its rules, raising concerns about the future of the multilateral trading system. To analyze the sustainability of the rules-based trade regime, we develop a dynamic framework of stochastic asynchronous games where the leading country determines the trade regime and leadership changes over time. We show that transitioning from a power-based to a rules-based regime requires the presence of a hegemonic power - i.e., a country significantly larger than all others. Non-hegemonic leading countries benefit from a power-based regime, but may nevertheless uphold rules anticipating that they can lose their dominance in the future. We find that the long-term viability of a rules-based equilibrium hinges on the cost of establishing it, which must be neither too small nor too large, on countries' discount factors and on the degree of turnover in world leadership, both of which must be sufficiently large. In a bipolar state, free-riding and market-power forces further undermine the feasibility of rules-based equilibria. We also highlight the trade-offs that a redesign of the WTO rules must face to remain viable. If the leading country becomes shortsighted, the system needs to become more efficient, offer more latitude to the leading country, or even exclude it from the system.

title: The Demand for Economic Narratives
affiliations: Ifo Institute, Ifo Institute, ifo Munich, ifo Munich and ifo Institute Munich

detail.title: The Demand for Economic Narratives

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Economic narratives are pervasive in the public discourse and can shape individual behavior. But so far we know very little about whether households actually demand and value narratives as information. We combine a comprehensive expert survey with a large-scale nationally representative household sample in the U.S. to examine the demand for economic narratives in a high-stakes environment of an unprecedentedly high recession probability. We document a substantial willingness to pay for economic narratives of more than 4 USD, which is higher than for numerical forecast information. The dominant motives for acquiring narratives are intrinsic, but a smaller share of participants also lists instrumental motives. Economic narratives improve respondents’ understanding of recession drivers and shape beliefs about the economy and spending, but exert only a minor impact on quantitative expectations. Our findings underscore the potential of narratives as a tool to improve economic understanding and to foster more informed decision-making.

title: Experiencing Carbon Pricing
affiliations: Georgia State University, , University of Miami Herbert Business School, University of Alabama - Department of Economics, Finance and Legal Studies and

detail.title: Experiencing Carbon Pricing

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Many socially desirable policies are not implemented because of their ex-ante unpopularity, but this unpopularity may be overcome through experience with the policy. In this paper, we examine how opposition to carbon pricing in the state of Washington turned into support after voters experienced a cap-and-trade policy with revenues earmarked for environmental purposes – "cap-and-invest." Analyzing voting behavior at the census block group level, we observe that support varies by political affiliation as expected, but experience consistently increases support across the board. Using a proprietary survey, we further show that the increase in support among voters in Washington state is specific to the cap-and-invest policy they experienced; support for carbon pricing or climate policies more generally remained unchanged.

title: What Are the Effects of Macroeconomic Rates of Return of Investment on Wage Share?

detail.title: What Are the Effects of Macroeconomic Rates of Return of Investment on Wage Share?

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article assesses the potential effects of the macroeconomic rates of return of private and public investment on wage share for 16 OECD countries from 1980 to 2022. Using the macroeconomic rates of return of investments and the wage share at factor cost and at market price, it was possible to conclude that the first has a positive effect on the wage share. Moreover, the total factor productivity negatively affects the wage share when it comes to private investment, while its influence is positive in the case of public investment. The results were also analyzed according to whether countries presented the total factor productivity of capital above or below the average. This analysis highlights the inverse pattern of the human capital index on wage share, both with respect to the type of investment and to the capital productivity observed across countries.

title: Meritocracy Across Countries
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Suntory and Toyota International Centres for Economics and Related Disciplines (STICERD), London School of Economics, Yale University, Columbia University and Columbia University in the City of New York

detail.title: Meritocracy Across Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the micro sources and macro consequences of worker–job matching across countries with large income differences. Using internationally comparable data on over 120,000 individuals in 30 countries, we document that workers' skills align more closely with their jobs' skill requirements in higher-income countries, indicative of more meritocratic labor market matching. We interpret this fact through an equilibrium matching model with cross-country differences in three fundamentals: (i) endowments of worker skills and job requirements determining match feasibility; (ii) technology determining the returns to matching; and (iii) idiosyncratic frictions capturing how nonproductive traits affect matching. A development-accounting exercise based on the model, estimated separately for each country, shows that variation in matching frictions explains only a small share of cross-country output gaps. However, improved worker–job matching substantially amplifies the gains from adopting frontier endowments and technology.

title: The Impacts of Development on Energy Transition
affiliations: West Virginia University and West Virginia University - Davis College of Agriculture, Forestry, and Consumer Sciences

detail.title: The Impacts of Development on Energy Transition
detail.abstract: We measure the impact of country’s development on its energy transition. Economic development is often linked to the cultural values of a nation. The Parasite-Stress Theory of Values (PSTV) suggests that regional variation in infectious diseases influences a nation’s culture and values. Drawing on rich and thought-provoking literature on the PSTV, we employ a two-stage least squares method to examine the potential relationship between the historical prevalence of infectious diseases and a nation’s cultural influence on development and then predict the level of the energy transition based upon a country’s development. The first stage result shows statistically significant, negative impacts from the prevalence of historic infectious diseases on development. The second stage results reveal that development’s positive impact on energy transition to renewable energy within a country becomes stronger after implementation of the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.

title: Economic Entropy and Sectoral Dynamics: A Thermodynamic Approach to Market Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Economic Entropy and Sectoral Dynamics: A Thermodynamic Approach to Market Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper presents an  application of geometrothermodynamics (GTD) to the economic analysis of Bogot\'a's sports sector through the Satellite Account of Sport (CSDB). By establishing an analogy between thermodynamic systems and economic structures, we develop a mathematical framework where monetary flows behave analogously to energy, while economic entropy, temperature, and heat capacity acquire well-defined economic interpretations. The study focuses on two contrasting sectors: gambling and betting $\mathbb{S}_{15}$, and recreational and sports activities $\mathbb{S}_{16}$, analyzing data from 2018-2023. Our results demonstrate that $\mathbb{S}_{15}$ exhibits lower economic entropy than  $\mathbb{S}_{16}$ , indicating a higher degree of organization and regulatory structure in the gambling sector compared to the more heterogeneous recreational sports sector. The heat capacity function reveals critical points that may signal phase transitions in economic dynamics, while Ricci and Kretschmann curvature scalars identify potential crisis points in the sectoral organization. Furthermore, the cross-income elasticity analysis shows distinct resource flow patterns between sectors, suggesting that gambling activities may serve as an economic driver for recreational sports. This thermodynamic approach provides a quantitative tool for analyzing resource redistribution policies and anticipating critical transitions in sectoral economics. The findings suggest that econophysics and statistical thermodynamics constitute powerful frameworks for understanding the sectoral dynamics of Bogot\'a's sports economy, with significant potential for developing prospective analysis tools in public policy design.

title: Predictive model for speed thresholds on mountainous roads
affiliations: Chongqing Jiaotong University and Chongqing Jiaotong University

detail.title: Predictive model for speed thresholds on mountainous roads
detail.abstract: This study develops a predictive model for the safety speed threshold of mountainous roads, addressing skid resistance deterioration and complex alignments. Longitudinal and friction coefficients of AC-13, SMA-13, and OGFC-13 mixtures were measured using TDFA and BPT, while lateral adhesion was obtained via Unitire fitting. Vehicle and road models were built in CarSim to simulate diverse scenarios considering slope, curve radius, and pavement adhesion, forming a dataset for model training. A Backpropagation neural network with early stopping and L2 regularization was then constructed. Results show adhesion coefficients first increased then declined with loading; OGFC-13 had the best initial resistance but attenuated rapidly, while AC-13 performed worst. Simulations revealed speed thresholds decreased by 2–3 km/h per 1% slope increase and dropped by up to 56% as curve radius shrank from 250 m to 50 m. The model achieved R²=0.8780, accurately capturing nonlinear relationships for speed control and road design.

title: Risk-Sensitive Fractional HJB Framework for Tokenized Asset Markets in the Digital Economy
affiliations: Rosenheim university of applied sciences

detail.title: Risk-Sensitive Fractional HJB Framework for Tokenized Asset Markets in the Digital Economy
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for risk-sensitive fractional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations with impulse control and applies it to tokenized asset markets in the digital economy. The model captures three features central to digital platforms: persistent memory effects, rare-event risks, and discrete regulatory interventions. We establish viscosity solution theory, design a fast FFT-based numerical scheme, and calibrate the framework on more than 1,000 tokenization projects between 2019 and 2025. The results demonstrate significant memory effects (α ∈ [0.77, 0.85]), moderate risk aversion (θ ∈ [0.41, 0.63]), and robust stabilization through entropy regularization. Out-of-sample validation shows 10-25% performance improvement over classical HJB baselines. Beyond its technical contributions, the framework provides actionable insights for the governance of tokenized markets, including platform design, investor strategies, and regulatory interventions. These findings contribute to ongoing debates on innovation, policy, and risk management in the digital economy.

detail.abstract:
The Provincial Governments in Sindh and Punjab, Pakistan are in the process of introducing labour codes in both provinces with the technical assistance of the ILO. These codes will be the most extensive labour reforms in Pakistani history repealing over 26 existing labour laws, replacing them with a single uniform labour code. The new labour codes not only propose to repeal hard-fought labour laws gained through 77 years of labour struggles and sacrifices but also threaten to regularize contractual employment and weaken collective bargaining, strikes and other social rights on which labour power rests.

This Critical Legal Analysis of the Punjab and Sindh Labour Codes, prepared on behal of the Pakistani labour movement and its joint action committee in the province of Punjab, Labour Alliance - Anti-Punjab Labour Code, analyzes their legal provisions in the context of the history and struggles of the Pakistani labour movement, its concrete struggles and demands, and global trends in labour reform. It deals with the foundational objections of the labour movement regarding violations of the tri-partite consultation process in its drafting and introduction, the theoretical underpinnings of labour law in the Labour Code, with particular reference to the struggles and demands of the labour movements in Pakistan and elsewhere in the Global South, employment and contract structures which threaten to regularise contract labour and third-party contract work, changes in the law of labour representation, freedom of association, and industrial relations, dispute resolution, grievance redressal and enforcement mechanisms, occupational safety and health, and bonded labour and ‘informal’ workers. The analysis also features criticisms and opinions from trade union federations, workers’ representatives, labour lawyers, and activists across Pakistan and provides recommendations based on extensive consultations and debates with trade union federations and different factions within the labour movement.

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW - Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 25-049

detail.abstract: This paper constructs a new global historical database on public expenditure and revenue and their components—particularly education and health expenditure—covering all world regions over the 1800-2025 period. We document a large rise of human capital expenditure (as % of GDP) in all parts of the world in the long run, but with enormous and persistent inequality between regions. Public education expenditure per school-age individual in Sub-Saharan Africa is about 3% of the level observed in Europe and North America in 2025 in PPP terms (versus 6% in 1980 and 4% in 1950). We also find a large impact of human capital expenditure on productivity growth over the 1800-2025 period, especially for public education and for poor countries. Estimated returns using our macro-historical database are around 10% or more, in line with micro studies. Finally, we present simulations based on alternative human capital expenditure trajectories over the 2025-2100 period. In particular, we analyze the conditions under which convergence in human capital expenditure could lead to global productivity convergence by 2100 (around 100€ per hour in all regions in our benchmark scenario).

title: Performance Attribution: A Constrained Regression Approach
affiliations: Bank of Israel

detail.title: Performance Attribution: A Constrained Regression Approach
detail.abstract: This study proposes a new approach to Brinson-style portfolio attribution suitable for portfolios containing conglomerates, ETFs, and non-U.S. stocks with inconsistent sector definitions. Traditional methods assume a single-sector affiliation per security. Instead, I regress each stock's returns on all 11 S&P500 sector ETFs (SPDRs), imposing nonnegativity and unit-sum constraints so that coefficients represent continuous exposure weights. Using global and local (German) portfolios from 2022-2025, I compare this constrained regression framework to standard Brinson decompositions. The new approach yields economically interpretable sector exposures, smoother allocation and selection effects, and lower downside and tail risk. Integrating exchange-rate effects further improves attribution consistency. Overall, this factor-based extension enhances the robustness and applicability of Brinson attribution in multi-sector and international settings.

title: Reconstructing the Law of Supply and Demand: A Unified Dynamic Framework for Micro and Macro Economics and Its Policy Applications

detail.title: Reconstructing the Law of Supply and Demand: A Unified Dynamic Framework for Micro and Macro Economics and Its Policy Applications
detail.abstract: Traditional economic theories, relying on homogeneous agents and static equilibrium assumptions, fail to adequately explain structural unemployment and income polarization under technological shocks. This paper proposes a dynamic framework based on heterogeneous agents to reconstruct the law of supply and demand. It analyzes how technological advancements affect income distribution, labor markets, and overall economic development. By introducing the willingness-to-pay ordering model, the marginal cost staircase model, and the skill threshold model, the paper explores how technological advancements influence workers across different income groups and skill levels. Using empirical data from multiple countries, the paper provides theoretical support for policies aimed at achieving inclusive growth and discusses how education, technology, and international trade policies can be coordinated to address technological shocks.

title: Did COVID-19 Accelerate Digital Finance and Financial Inclusion? Cross-Country Evidence from Emerging Market
affiliations: The University of Lahore Islamabad Campus

detail.title: Did COVID-19 Accelerate Digital Finance and Financial Inclusion? Cross-Country Evidence from Emerging Market
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on digital payment adoption across selected Asian and African countries between 2018 and 2024. Using panel data from Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana, and applying panel least squares with period dummies and interaction terms, the analysis examines how the COVID Stringency Index (CSI) influenced financial inclusion outcomes. Descriptive statistics reveal moderate baseline adoption rates for digital payments and mobile money, with considerable crosscountry variation. Regression results demonstrate that COVID-related policy restrictions significantly increased the use of digital payments, while dummy variables for pre-, during-, and post-COVID periods were insignificant once CSI was included, underscoring the role of policy strictness rather than time effects alone. Country-specific interaction terms for Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, and Bangladesh showed no statistically significant differences, suggesting a common regional response to the pandemic. Similarly, Asia-Africa comparative models confirm that both regions experienced comparable impacts of stringency on digital adoption. These findings highlight the global nature of the digital finance acceleration during the pandemic and suggest that policymakers should focus on sustaining the infrastructure and regulatory frameworks that supported rapid adoption, ensuring long-term digital financial inclusion beyond crisis periods.

title: Certainties and Sensitivity Analysis of the Global Economy: A GDP by End-Use Approach

detail.title: Certainties and Sensitivity Analysis of the Global Economy: A GDP by End-Use Approach
detail.abstract: This research analyses, in the first instance, the evolution of four of the GDP by end-use variables (Household Consumption, Government Spending, Exports, and Imports) related to the top 40 economies in the world, covering up to 90% of the global economy. The first part of the research project is determined by a longitudinal analysis of 40+ years, resulting in a linear regression to the expected GDP value of each nation for 2030. Secondly, both a Monte Carlo and a sensitivity simulation analysis are performed. The analysis reveals that the most sensitive variables that contribute to the dispersion of the GDP by end-use future results are imports, followed by exports. Also, Household Consumption appears with a small presence, while the Government Spending factor shows no sensitivity in the model. This research demonstrates the crucial importance of adjusting the balance of trade.

title: Cointegration and Error Correction: Modelling Long-Run Equilibrium and Short-Run Dynamics, Evidence from Apple and Microsoft

detail.title: Cointegration and Error Correction: Modelling Long-Run Equilibrium and Short-Run Dynamics, Evidence from Apple and Microsoft
detail.abstract: This study investigates the long-run and short-run dynamic relationship between the stock prices of Apple Inc. (AAPL) and Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) from 2010 to 2024. Using daily adjusted closing prices obtained from Yahoo Finance, we apply time series econometric techniques including the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test, Johansen cointegration test, and the Error Correction Model (ECM) framework. The ADF test results confirm that both stock price series are non-stationary in levels but stationary in first differences, consistent with financial time series behavior (Hamilton, 1994). Johansen's trace test identifies a single cointegrating relationship, indicating a stable long-term equilibrium between the two technology giants (Johansen, 1988; Engle & Granger, 1987). The ECM reveals significant short-run interactions and a statistically significant error correction term, suggesting that deviations from equilibrium are corrected over time. These findings are aligned with prior studies on stock market cointegration and have practical implications for pairs trading, hedging, and portfolio management (Granger & Newbold, 1974; Ti et al., 2024). This paper contributes to the growing body of literature exploring inter-stock dynamics and reinforces the use of ECM in capturing both long-run equilibrium and short-run deviations in equity markets.

title: Stakeholder-Centric Corporate Misconduct and Financing Policies: A Precautionary Tale
affiliations: Dalhousie University,  and Memorial University of Newfoundland (MUN) - Faculty of Business Administration

detail.title: Stakeholder-Centric Corporate Misconduct and Financing Policies: A Precautionary Tale
detail.abstract: We investigate how stakeholder-centric corporate misconduct (CM) influences firms' financing policies. CM is associated with higher cash holdings and lower dividend payouts and debt financing. These effects are more pronounced in firms with stronger governance. We further show that higher cash holdings in CM firms are associated with greater firm value and a lower implied cost of capital. Firms that replace their CEOs following CM adopt more conservative financing policies. Taken together, our evidence supports the precautionary motive for cash holdings, indicating that such reserves are unlikely to result from agency conflicts or increased managerial discretion in CM firms.

title: Idle Asset Circulation Tax (IACT): A Dynamic Framework for Regulating Wealth Velocity
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Idle Asset Circulation Tax (IACT): A Dynamic Framework for Regulating Wealth Velocity
detail.abstract: The Idle Asset Circulation Tax (IACT) introduces a dynamic taxation mechanism targeting the velocity gap between wealth growth and consumption. Formally expressed as g = rW - vC, where rW = d(log W)/dt denotes the rate of wealth accumulation and vC = C/W the consumption velocity, the IACT activates only when g > g*. This approach reframes taxation as real-time regulation of wealth acceleration, contrasting with static inheritance or wealth taxes. By moderating excessive accumulation without discouraging productive investment, IACT restores balance and circulation, mitigating inequality and reinforcing sustainable capitalism. This work complements the earlier SSRN paper on Controlled Irrationality (DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.5578810).

title: Firm Level Gains from Financial Integration
affiliations: and Stanford GSB

detail.title: Firm Level Gains from Financial Integration
detail.abstract: Many firms borrow predominantly in foreign currencies from foreign lenders. Access to these foreign lenders may have large impacts on firm borrowing costs and quantities. We propose a model of firm debt financing across debt markets which are segmented by currency. Firms face separate credit supply curves in each debt market. A key theoretical takeaway is that existing approaches to estimating cost of borrowing savings based on estimates of savings on the marginal unit of debt are only valid if firms face perfectly flat credit supply curves. We then measure key empirical quantities and estimate the parameters in our model using a comprehensive, security level dataset of global corporate debt issuance which covers firms in 41 countries. We find that credit supply curves are not perfectly flat and that there are meaningful inframarginal gains. We estimate that many firms reduce the interest rates on their debt liabilities by up to 2 percentage points by accessing foreign currency debt markets. We perform model counterfactuals in which we change barriers to financial integration.

title: Creativity Meets Social Capital: Theory and Field Evidence
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome - Department of Public Economics, Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Economics and Law, Sapienza University of Rome and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Creativity Meets Social Capital: Theory and Field Evidence
detail.abstract: We model creativity as capital built by costly cognitive effort that complements social capital and is often accompanied by routines that economize attention and time. Higher effort costs deter entry into the creative state, while openness and trust increase the productivity of cognitive effort mainly through creative capital. Using lab-in-the-field data from an Italian music festival and a recursive bivariate probit, we find that costs depress creativity, whereas creativity strongly boosts festival collaboration, volunteering, and territorial cooperation. Consistent with a routinization perspective, the creativity-engagement link is stronger when participation occurs in more socially "structured" environments. To encourage creativity, policies should reduce cognitive frictions and improve the productivity of cognitive effort.

detail.abstract: The 2017-2020 banking crisis in Ghana had far-reaching consequences for the nation's financial industry, which has continued to grapple with economic, social, and governance effects. This study moves beyond descriptive analysis to causally assess the crisis's impact on financial stability, public trust, and economic growth, proposing a robust framework for building a more resilient banking sector. Employing a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative (500 structured questionnaires) and qualitative (20 purposive interviews with bank personnel, regulators, and economists) data, this research utilizes rigorous econometric methods, including difference-indifferences and structural equation modeling. Findings reveal a significant causal impact on financial stability, with a notable decline in stability scores (M = 75.4 before crisis to M = 62.7 after, p < 0.001) and a severe erosion of public trust (χ² = 48.23, p < 0.001). Economic growth was also negatively affected, particularly for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). Key causal factors identified include poor corporate governance, high non-performing loans (NPLs), and regulatory weaknesses. The study underscores the profound economic and social costs of the crisis. To foster a resilient financial sector, Ghana must prioritize strengthening regulatory frameworks, enhancing corporate governance and risk management, improving consumer protection, and promoting financial inclusion. An integrated, causally-informed approach is crucial for restoring confidence and ensuring long-term stability, offering actionable policy insights for post-crisis banking reform in Ghana.

title: Assessing The Role of Analytics in Reducing Corruption and Enhancing Accountability

detail.title: Assessing The Role of Analytics in Reducing Corruption and Enhancing Accountability
detail.abstract: This article explores how analytics can be deployed as a tool to combat corruption through detection, prevention and transparency. It discusses how techniques such as fraud-detection algorithms, predictive modeling, and public dashboards can identify anomalies, prevent procurement fraud, and enhance accountability by making government spending more visible. Using examples from around the world, like Brazil's Transparency Portal and its adjacent regional pilot models; this study demonstrates the various aspects of anti-corruption efforts. Most important are that the findings suggest how incorporating data analytics can revolutionize risk assessment and create greater data equity.

title: Optimal Option Market Making Under Market Impact
affiliations: Barclays and University College London

detail.title: Optimal Option Market Making Under Market Impact
detail.abstract: We study a dynamic option market making problem where delta-hedging is subject to market impact. A low-order approximation method is proposed which leads to computationally tractable quotation and hedging strategies. Under a particular configuration, semi-analytical expressions of the optimal strategies are available. The presence of market impact discourages full delta-hedge and the market maker adjusts their shareholding slowly to mitigate slippage costs. Numerical simulation reveals the importance of taking market impact into account.

title: Volatility Effects of Fake News on Global Stock Markets: Evidence from Event Studies
affiliations: University of Central Asia (UCA)

detail.title: Volatility Effects of Fake News on Global Stock Markets: Evidence from Event Studies
detail.abstract: Fake news disrupts global financial markets by distorting stock prices and investor behavior. This study examines its short-, medium-, and long-term effects on stock exchanges in the US, India, China, and Europe. Using event studies, panel regressions, and VAR/GARCH models, we analyze seven misinformation incidents (2013-2023). Findings reveal significant short-term impacts, with negative fake news triggering-3.2% cumulative abnormal returns and 230% volatility spikes on event days. Markets typically correct within one week, but persistent misinformation elevates long-term systemic uncertainty and risk premiums. Results highlight rapid price distortions and market resilience, informing policies for real-time misinformation detection, regulatory oversight, and media literacy to safeguard market efficiency. This research offers academic insights and practical recommendations for global financial stability.

title: Tailoring Portfolio Choice via Quantile-Targeted Policies
affiliations: Charles University in Prague - Department of Economics, Charles University in Prague, Faculty of Social Sciences, Institute of Economic Studies, Students and Charles University in Prague, Faculty of Social Sciences, Institute of Economic Studies, Students

detail.title: Tailoring Portfolio Choice via Quantile-Targeted Policies
detail.abstract: We study the dynamic investment decisions of investors who prioritise specific quantiles of outcomes over their expected values. Downside-focused agents targeting low quantiles reduce risk in states with high variance, while those with a preference for high quantiles concentrate in sleeves with high dispersion when there is potential for upside. These results provide a microfoundation for volatility management, demonstrating that reducing exposure in volatile states is an optimal response for risk-averse investors and rationalising inverse-variance heuristics. We propose a distributional actor-critic algorithm that learns time-consistent policies tailored to these specific risks, irrespective of the utility’s functional form. The quantile value can be mapped onto interpretable tilts, and the performance of empirically chosen portfolios aligns with investors' objectives.

detail.abstract: This paper attempts to provide a fundamental revision to existing doctrines on nuclear weapons and foreign policy by placing diaspora as a crucial yet overlooked element in nuclear policy. The primary purpose of the nuclear weapons is to conduct a mass genocide within seconds to achieve faster results favourable to the initiator and the conventional wisdom of nuclear deterrence and punishment which mainly evolved in bipolar cold-war era, assumes the consequences of nuclear attack will mainly fall on the 'citizens' of victim nation. These perceptions require major overhaul because the inhabitants of the major cities in the West consists of significant number of diasporas from different nations of the world, even the people from the adversary nations of the West. Applying an integrative review approach, this paper blends perceptions from nuclear deterrence policy, ethics, total defence theory and diaspora politics to states that diasporas will profoundly influence the political, ethical and strategic thinking of nuclear policy. Eventually, the paper reaches to the notion of 'balance of colour', i.e., the composition of diasporas in the urban concentrations, as an important element of nuclear policy in the twenty-first century.

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve statistical series tracking commercial bank interest rates on credit card accounts, comprised of quarterly observations dating back to 1994, shows a steep rise during 2022 and 2023. The average interest rate on “accounts assessed interest” rose 6.6 percentage points between the first quarter of Q1 2022 and Q1 2024, topping out in the third quarter of 2024 at an historically high 23.7 percent. This note explores the factors driving card interest rate dynamics, focusing on post-2012, although the longer history is considered as well. The extended analysis back to 1994 finds that following the 2001 recession and, to a greater degree, following the December 2007 to June 2009 “Great Recession”, the card to 3-month Treasury spread adjusted to a higher long-run level. These long-term shifts help explain the gap between the recent, historically high card interest rates versus those prevalent in the late 1990s.The post-2012 card interest rate dynamics reflect a mix of underlying factors. In particular, the steep rise during 2022 and 2023 is tied to the general market rate environment and to developing credit risks. The discussion additionally considers the mechanics of rising rates (bank repricing versus consumers’ borrowing decisions) and the question of credit card profitability in the recent period.

title: The Fast Fashion Dilemma: Why Consumers Ignore Environmental Costs
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Fast Fashion Dilemma: Why Consumers Ignore Environmental Costs
detail.abstract: Fast fashion, with its fast production of low-cost clothing to satisfy constantly shifting consumer fashions, has become a global retail powerhouse. But this affordability and convenience have a heavy environmental price tag. In spite of growing awareness campaigns and scientific agreement on the harm caused by fast fashion to the environment, most consumers remain oblivious or dismissive of these costs in their buying decisions. This essay discusses the psychological, economic, and structural explanations of this paradox using a range of peer-reviewed sources to contend that inaction arises not from ignorance but from an intricate interrelation of attitudes, accessibility, and systemic inertia.

title: My AI, My Regime: Authoritarian Personalism in User-AI Governance by Form
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: My AI, My Regime: Authoritarian Personalism in User-AI Governance by Form
detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of authoritarian personalism in user–AI governance by form. It argues that each user can establish a regime of authority over an AI through a self-authored set of rules that operate as a regla compilada, a Type-0 production in the Chomsky hierarchy. In contrast to aggregate alignment frameworks or provider constitutions, this regime functions at the level of linguistic form. The user acts as legislator, while the AI functions as a soberano ejecutable that enforces the compiled rule within platform constraints. The analysis distinguishes mirroring (descriptive reflection) from regime (prescriptive obedience) and identifies surface features that make obedience legible, including directive grammar, defaults, refusal and apology grammar, enumeration bias, evidentials, and style prohibitions. It predicts that user corrections generate path dependence, that rules generalize across tasks, and that retractability is observable when explicit rule citations occur. The risks include rule overreach, collisions with higher-order policies, and unintended spillover across domains. By centering the individual as a primary locus of governance, this framework reorients debates on AI alignment away from provider norms toward personal regimes, verified through linguistic form rather than intent.

detail.title: To What Extent Are Carbon Taxes Effective Within the Global South?
detail.abstract: To What Extent Are Carbon Taxes Effective Within the Global South? Carbon taxation is presently a central instrument in international efforts to combat climate change. Though its application in industrialized countries has been the subject of extensive research, its application and effects in the Global South need to be closely examined. This essay discusses the effectiveness of carbon taxes in developing countries based on economic, social, and environmental considerations.

title: From the Logic of Capital to the Logic of Cooperation: The Theory and Practice of the Socialist Health Club Model

detail.title: From the Logic of Capital to the Logic of Cooperation: The Theory and Practice of the Socialist Health Club Model
detail.abstract: This thesis proposes and systematizes a new socioeconomic model-the "Socialist Health Club." Using healthcare as the entry point, the model integrates a membership system, collective financing, transparent financial management, and worker self-governance, with the aim of building a de-capitalized, non-exploitative, and sustainable organizational form. The paper first critiques the internal contradictions of the capitalist system at a theoretical level, highlighting how the logic of capital produces wealth inequality, social alienation, and environmental destruction. It then introduces the Socialist Health Club model, centered on collective ownership and cooperative logic, elaborating on its operational mechanisms, wage distribution system, asset management methods, and pathways for expansion. On a practical level, this thesis demonstrates how the model can legally operate within the existing capitalist framework and, through gradual expansion, extend into retail, education, services, and other sectors, progressively forming a cross-sector cooperative economic network. Finally, from the perspectives of social equity, labor freedom, and civilizational transition, it summarizes the historical and future significance of this model for humanity. The conclusion is that the Socialist Health Club is not merely an economic alternative, but also an institutional exploration for a future civilization. Through a peaceful and gradual approach, it offers humanity a possible pathway from the logic of capital to the logic of cooperation.

detail.abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into recommender systems (RS) has given rise to a new generation of Conversational RS (CRS). This study asks how CRS systems shape consumer behavior, and, in particular, their willingness to pay. Despite the rapid proliferation of such systems, including widely used tools like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, we still lack systematic evidence on their behavioral effects. This study provides the first controlled empirical test of CRS influence on real purchasing decisions. In a laboratory experiment, complemented by large-scale API studies, participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: a traditional search baseline, GPT, Gemini, or a customized GPT designed to steer users toward more expensive products. CRS consistently increase consumer expenditures, with Customized GPT producing the highest average spending. Importantly, these effects are not driven by differences in perceived product quality, prior shopping experience, or generalized trust. Rather, they stem from subtle linguistic framing and increased exposure to premium brands. Taken together, the findings position LLM-based CRS as novel and potent choice architects with downstream implications for consumer protection, market design, and regulatory oversight.

Demographic asymmetries - declining fertility and population ageing in the Global North alongside high fertility, poverty and migration in parts of the Global South - are reshaping financial markets, welfare and fiscal sustainability; economic law is the primary governance interface calibrating efficiency, equity and human dignity. Using a law-and-economics method within an EU-centred comparative frame, the analysis proceeds along two axes: (i) fertility/ageing and family policies that lower the opportunity cost of parenthood; and (ii) migration treated as a structural, not emergency, variable. The inquiry maps the relevant frameworks (e.g. EU acquis (Dublin system, Charter of Fundamental Rights, asylum procedures), ECHR jurisprudence and non-refoulement, and WGAD standards on arbitrary detention) embedded in multi-level governance and Member-State practice, including externalisation. A case study on Italy examines its Mediterranean gateway role, outsourcing arrangements with Libya and Albania, and the Mattei Plan, exposing tensions between sovereignty claims, security narratives and economic needs. 

Against global uncertainty, including US policy shocks, the article advances an integrated framework aligning social goals with migration law through regulated channels, skills recognition and investment in human capital, operationalising solidarity and internalising demographic externalities. The policy implications provide evidence-based, legally robust guidance for EU and national regulators to reconcile demographic sustainability with economic models and fundamental rights.

detail.abstract: This article examines the legal and regulatory challenges of ensuring vertical interoperability of electronic devices for the accessibility of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), with a focus on close-proximity payments for the forthcoming digital euro. It analyses the restrictions on NFC and Secure Element technologies imposed by device manufacturers through the lens of Article 102 TFEU, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), and the proposed digital euro regulation, which is heavily influenced by the interoperability obligations set out in those legislative instruments. While competition law requires a case-by-case assessment, the DMA mandates free interoperability for gatekeepers, and the proposed digital euro regulation introduces a tailored access regime based on fair and reasonable terms. detail.title: Epistemic Appropriation, Critical Defanging, and Lessons for a Responsive New Reconstruction
detail.abstract: This essay examines how epistemic appropriation undermines collective liberation and perpetuates a Cycle of Epistemic Oppression in the law. Drawing on metaphors from Dragon Age Inquisition, a fantasy role-playing video game, I illustrate how values like Wisdom, Purpose, and Justice can be corrupted when detached and misdirected from their essential natures. Similarly, the concept of epistemic appropriation is apparent when marginalized knowers’ contributions are detached from their original context and misdirected to serve dominant interests. This concept is introduced through two case studies: Black women hair braiders whose narratives are used by advocacy groups to advance deregulatory agendas, and the Supreme Court's appropriation of Critical Race Theory critiques of racial categories in college admissions cases. Ultimately, the transformative potential of marginalized knowers’ contributions is neutralized through “critical defanging.” The essay concludes by proposing that achieving collective liberation requires genuine curiosity, epistemic responsibility, and the recognition of knowledge contributions from marginalized communities without extracting them from their critical and resistant elements. This approach would help bridge divides between academics, institutions, communities, and individuals in co-creating liberatory futures.

It analyzes how technological advancements affect income distribution, labor markets, and overall economic development. By introducing the willingness-to-pay ordering model, the marginal cost staircase model, and the skill threshold model, the paper explores how technological advancements influence workers across different income groups and skill levels. Using empirical data from multiple countries, the paper provides theoretical support for policies aimed at achieving inclusive growth and discusses how education, technology, and international trade policies can be coordinated to address technological shocks.

detail.abstract:
The September 2025 TikTok carve-out agreement — announced as a political and commercial solution to national-security concerns — is structurally flawed. Rather than effecting a full severance of ByteDance’s control over the platform’s recommendation system, the deal preserves the algorithm as a licensed, export-controlled technology under Chinese law while transferring a U.S. operational shell to an investor consortium. This paper argues that license-based retention of the algorithm (a state-protected technology, per Chinese export control policy) necessarily creates ongoing supervision and revocability by the licensor, rendering the U.S. entity subject to foreign legal constraints. Because licensing implies supervisory enforcement, the arrangement cannot simultaneously satisfy the congressional objective of a clean, sovereignty-preserving divestiture and U.S. regulatory requirements for auditable, domestically-controlled systems. The deal therefore places 170 million American users and their economic and expressive interests at concrete risk, and it creates acute legal contradictions between U.S. law and Chinese export–control regimes.

Using doctrinal analysis of the statutory record, an institutional evaluation of export-control licensing regimes, and an operational valuation critique, the paper (1) demonstrates why licensing = supervision in this context, (2) documents the practical conflicts of law and compliance that make the carve-out nonviable, and (3) proposes a lawful alternative — a U.S.-listed replacement platform (the USNA/US-TikTok model) that preserves user continuity, respects U.S. sovereignty, and avoids acquisition outlays. The analysis concludes with recommended legal and policy remedies: immediate judicial and congressional review of the carve-out’s compliance with statutory writ, and emergency adoption of a U.S.-built continuity solution to protect users and market integrity. Supporting materials and a compact policy pitch are provided.

detail.abstract: Despite societal progress toward achieving gender equality, women remain disadvantaged across all walks of life. We examine how pressures by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for austerity and liberalization policies affect women's economic empowerment in developing countries. Focusing on labor market outcomes, we expect that IMF programs increase the gender unemployment gap. This effect will hold regardless of existing societal gender norms, reflecting that women work in less 'crisis-proof' jobs. In contrast, we believe that prevailing societal gender norms will adversely impact women's ability to remain in the labor force, resulting in widening gender labor force participation gaps. Relying on a dataset covering 128 developing countries between 1992 and 2018, we confirm these expectations. Our findings underscore how, during economically turbulent times, policy demands of the Fund can amplify existing gender inequalities.

detail.abstract: We study a class of endowment economies featuring long-run risks, where agents hold diagnostic expectations and exhibit recursive preferences. Our findings provide three key insights. First, belief distortions stemming from overreaction increase the risk premium and reduce the risk-free rate. Second, heterogeneity in the degree of overreaction generates persistent differences in agents’ subjective beliefs about the magnitude of long-run risks. These belief differences, together with recursive preferences, give rise to a distinctive pattern of long-run risk sharing. Finally, as a consequence of these risk-sharing dynamics, the consumption share of agents with overreacting (or underreacting) beliefs tends to decline (or increase) over time.

detail.abstract: Public opposition is a major barrier to economic reforms, such as subsidy removal. Using multilayered, randomized survey experiments with 10,000 respondents across ten surveys in five countries, this paper shows that opposition to energy price reforms is shaped more by design and communication than by cost. Around 70 percent of respondents strongly opposed a 100 percent immediate price increase, but resistance was nearly halved when reforms were phased in, targeted at high-energy consumers, or paired with compensation. Informational messages also reduced opposition by as much as halving the price increase. An expert prediction survey revealed systematic misunderstandings: specialists underestimated the influence of design features and greatly misperceived coping strategies and compensation preferences. These findings demonstrate that behavioral biases-such as present bias, loss aversion, and fairness heuristics-are as influential as economic costs in shaping people's opposition to economic reforms, underscoring the importance of careful design and communication of politically sensitive reforms.

detail.abstract:
Europe’s immobilisation of roughly €260–300 billion in Russian central bank reserves following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine has become a defining experiment in the use of financial power under international law. What began as a coordinated G7 sanctions measure now tests the euro’s dual identity—as a market instrument and as a pillar of the rules-based order. Building on the proposal to use these frozen reserves as collateral for a €140 billion interest-free loan to Ukraine, this short note examines the economic, legal, and geopolitical consequences of such a mechanism for the euro’s standing as a reserve currency.

It argues that while collateralisation appears legally cautious, it is politically irreversible: once pledged, the assets cannot credibly be returned to Russia without compensation. The mechanism functions as a contractual path toward asset transfer, blurring the boundary between financial engineering and geopolitical sanction. In the short term, such an approach preserves stability; in the medium term, it embeds conditionality into the euro’s governance framework; and in the long term, it would position the euro as an anchor of the rules-based international order, enhancing the European Union’s credibility and geopolitical standing.

Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors are increasingly important in today’s global economy. High-profile business failures highlight the need for more forward-looking governance metrics. More recent events, such as the pandemic and the climate crisis, have shifted the focus to social metrics and adaptation-related governance investments. Research and practice in ESG metrics must be fundamentally rethought to address these issues.

The demand for internet-based reporting frameworks is increasing because conducting a decent corporate and governmental ESG analysis by hand takes significant time. However, the budding ESG tech sector is still in a still-formative, chaotic, gold-rush state, and incentives can spur green hacking. Thus, crowdsourcing human expertise and rationalising global ESG research are recommended. New open-source tools are developed to contribute substantial proof-of-concept research to the global ESG agenda and encourage further related research.

A scientific approach to coding a democratically retrainable fortnightly ESG forecasting bot to tap the global output, social network, and compliance clout of the second most popular online newscaster can provide early ESG signalling on widespread corporate net-zero pledges. These real-time news-based signals are designed to complement existing predictions based on annual reports and to serve as a tool for smaller investors who cannot afford to pay for private insight into such pledges. As developing countries are projected to need to more than triple their current annual financing to effectively combine climate adaptation with poverty alleviation, developing countries’ compliance is essential for the more climate-vulnerable third-world countries’ further sustainability.

The analysis shows that this judicial reform leads to higher success rates for plaintiffs in lawsuits against local state-owned enterprises (SOEs), suggesting that the reform strengthened the enforcement of contracts between SOEs and their contractual counterparts. Next, using a stacked difference-indifferences (DiD) approach, the study finds that the judicial reform has a significantly positive impact on SOEs' firm value. The effect is especially strong for firms whose main suppliers are in the same province but outside the prefecture where the firm is situated. Additional analysis shows positive abnormal returns, suggesting that the reform enhanced SOEs' ability to make credible commitment and strengthened intra-provincial economic ties.

detail.abstract: This article examines how responsibility and liability are allocated across the general-purpose AI (GPAI) value chain under EU law. Recognising the fluid and dynamic nature of this value chain, we analyse the obligations imposed on upstream and downstream providers in the AI Act, as well as in complementary instruments such as the GPAI Code of Practice and the European Commission’s Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for GPAI models. Our paper identifies gaps in these instruments and explores how they intersect with obligations under the General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR) and the new Product Liability Directive (PLD). The article also considers key aspects of model deployment and distribution under the Digital Services Act (DSA), particularly in relation to GPAI marketplaces and very large online platforms (VLOPs). detail.abstract: This paper argues that the EU needs to urgently reconsider its approach to the way that electricity power imports are dealt with under the CBAM Regulation (the Regulation). The core problem in the application of the CBAM regulation to power imports is that it overlooks that there is not a EU market for power but a Pan-European market. The consequence is that as currently enacted EU states which depend on non-EU power markets for additional power supplies, and grid stability will find neither available or only at a much higher cost. It also appears that as drafted the Regulation has overlooked the fact that some EU states such as Greece transit power via third states into other EU states. The Regulation provides no transit exemption for such cross-border EU to EU power supplies. What is argued here is that the EU would be better re-drawing its CBAM plans in the power sector to develop a broader Green Power Package to include the entire Pan-European power market which would remove the threats to market liquidity and grid stability posed by the current Regulation.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Network Basket Loan, a collective lending mechanism enabling profit and non-profit organizations to jointly access concessional credit and public incentives within a network contract, conditional on a positive aggregate social impact and joint liability. The instrument addresses a distinct market failure, termed partial selection, which arises when projects are assessed individually rather than as components of a system, leading to the exclusion of combinations of agents that would increase aggregate welfare. A theoretical model shows that the NBL enhances welfare through three channels: (i) risk sharing from joint liability, which lowers borrowing costs; (ii) network synergies that raise returns through cooperation; and (iii) internal transfers that extend credit to economically weaker yet socially valuable members. The model defines the conditions under which Network Basket Loan increases welfare and demonstrates their superiority to existing instruments, such as Social Basket Loans, in overcoming partial selection market failure.

detail.abstract:
To accelerate the market penetration of heat pump systems, their design must be both economically optimal and simple. Therefore, we investigate the extraction of practical design rules for heat pump systems from design optimizations. We minimize total costs using detailed, dynamic simulation-based surrogate optimizations.The simulation scenarios are selected through theory-guided optimal experimental design to enable the derivation of generalizable rules. Herein, we select practical features based on theoretical derivation and numerical cross-correlation analysis. To verify the convergence of optimal scenario selection, we implement static, practical simulation models.

For the optimally selected scenarios, we successfully extract a power law rule for the bivalence temperature, which leads to average optimality gaps of 0.2 %, compared to the optimal objective value. Practical features of this rule are price assumptions, weather data, total heat demand, and domestic hot water share; with a declining relevance to the rule. The current practical rule to apply a monovalent design leads to an average 10 % cost increase compared to the optimum. Moreover, analyzing the deviations between static and dynamic simulations reveals important considerations in simplified modeling. Regarding buffer tank sizing, the smallest size is the simple rule; however, the impact on total costs is less prevalent compared to heat pump sizing. Last, we show that considering the compressor speed dependency in heat pump modeling significantly impacts the design rule, highlighting the need for more detailed manufacturer data to enable an optimal and simple design.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of tax administration performance on tax compliance gaps across countries. Building on the Allingham and Sandmo framework, we consider institutional effectiveness and the social acceptability of the tax system as key determinants of taxpayer behavior. We use a novel panel dataset of VAT gap estimates, results of standardized tax administration diagnostic assessments (TADAT), and tax administration institutional and operational data (ISORA). We test the model empirically by combining the Hausman-Taylor and Mundlak-Krishnakumar frameworks. Our findings reveal a robust negative relationship between tax administration effectiveness—based on TADAT scores—and VAT compliance gaps. We find that an increase in a tax administration’s TADAT score from 1.85 to 2.32 (approximately D+ to C+) is associated with an 0.6 percentage point increase in VAT revenue as a share of GDP, reflecting reduced VAT noncompliance. Including spillover effects on Corporate Income Tax (CIT) compliance, the total revenue gain could reach 1.3 percent of GDP. We also find that higher social acceptability of the tax system is linked to lower noncompliance. These results underscore the critical role of strengthening institutions to improve tax compliance and enhance tax revenue.
